name: Salisbury diet

lead: The Salisbury diet was promoted by the American physician and chemist James H. Salisbury (1823-1905). It centres on lean beef shaped into patties, which he called muscle pulp of beef, eaten with little plant food and accompanied by hot water.

It matters to appearance communities as a precursor to modern high-protein and carnivore diets, and bodybuilders have compared it to later steak-and-eggs plans. Salisbury designed it for digestive disorders, and published research on it is limited to historical accounts.

paras: Historical descriptions call for lean beef trimmed of fat and gristle, shaped into cakes about half an inch to an inch thick and broiled slowly, seasoned with butter, salt, pepper or simple condiments, with vegetables kept minimal. The hot water accompanied meals. Modern lifters who mention it usually refer loosely to a ground-beef-centred routine.

The plan excludes most plant foods, so fibre, vitamin and variety considerations apply. It was designed as a therapeutic regimen in the 1800s, and clinicians today generally advise people with kidney, cardiovascular or digestive conditions to consult a professional before a very high-meat diet.

lead: The Salisbury diet is a meat-based regimen named after James H. Salisbury (1823-1905), an American physician and chemist who promoted it as a treatment for digestive complaints and a route to health.[1] The centrepiece is the Salisbury steak, a patty of lean beef muscle trimmed of fat and connective tissue, broiled and eaten with minimal vegetables.[1]

For appearance, the diet is relevant as an early example of a protein-dominant plan. Bodybuilding forums mention it in discussions of simple ground-beef eating, comparing it with Vince Gironda's steak-and-eggs approach.[2] Modern commentary frames it as a historical precursor of high-protein and carnivore-style diets rather than a current programme.

The name Salisbury steak for a beef patty main course has been in American use since 1897, and the dish is now associated with gravy, mashed potatoes and frozen dinners, a different meaning from the original diet.[1]

paras: Salisbury called the patty muscle pulp of beef. His recipe used lean muscle with fat, gristle and connective tissue removed, shaped into cakes about half an inch to an inch thick and broiled slowly without smoke. Seasonings were butter, salt, pepper and optional condiments such as mustard, horseradish, lemon juice or Worcestershire sauce, and celery was allowed sparingly.[1]

The patty descends from German Hamburg steak, brought to America by emigrants through Hamburg in the early 1800s. The Salisbury steak name has been used in the US since 1897.[1] A 1951 article in Postgraduate Medicine, titled for Salisbury steak, hamburger and the Salisbury diet, records the historical interest in his work.[3]

On the T Nation forum, a 2024 thread about eating a pound of ground beef notes that the idea is not far from Vince Gironda's steak-and-eggs diet or the original Salisbury diet.[2] Forum references to Salisbury steak in contest-prep logs generally mean the meal rather than the historical regimen.[4]
No studies found. Modern research on high-protein and low-carbohydrate diets exists, but no trial has tested the Salisbury regimen specifically.

lore.intro: Forum mentions are brief and usually place the diet alongside other meat-centred plans.[2]
